# sisakulint terms

- commit: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567

## item names

The item names are the names listed below. Most item names start an item of a list in --explain, followed by a colon and then what the item name names (such as problem: ...). An ID may come between the item name and the colon (such as precondition attacker-writes: ...). Some item names are within the text of an item, in parentheses or after a comma, followed by what they name, with a colon or without one (such as decided by: run-time, from VC, VI and runner 2.337.0). Some item names are also the heading of a group of values under values (such as severity and disposition). Other words before a colon are not item names: an ID (of a finding kind, a fix kind, a form, an inconclusive kind, a precondition or an incident), the name of a CVSS metric (such as AV), the name of an axis of the facets (such as weakness), and a value (such as always in default run: always: ...). When the value of an item name is empty, --explain leaves out the whole item, the item name together with the value: for example, a rule or a kind without fixes has no item fix kinds.

- commit: the commit of git the binary was built from, marked (modified) when the working tree had changes; unknown when it is not known
- terms: the command that writes these terms
- problem: what the rule detects, and why it is a problem
- expected: the state that the rule asks for (the ideal). The rule reports a finding where a workflow departs from the state, and reports nothing where the workflow keeps the state, with three exceptions: where a workflow has an undetected form, the rule reports nothing, even where the workflow departs from the state; on the places of an inconclusive kind, the rule cannot decide whether the workflow departs from the state, or whether the consequence of a finding kind of the rule can occur at the place, and the rule reports a finding whose certainty is inconclusive (an inconclusive finding); where a workflow has a false positive form, the rule reports a finding though the consequence of the finding kind does not occur in the workflow, even where the workflow keeps the state. The declaration of each form and of each inconclusive kind gives the reason: the disposition, or, for a false positive form, the disposition or the fact kinds. Whether a finding is a false positive is decided by the consequence of the finding kind, not by the state: a finding where the workflow departs from the state is a false positive too when the consequence of the finding kind does not occur in the workflow
- severity: how bad a threat is on any repository, not the risk to one organization: the severity of a kind is found from the CVSS metrics of the kind by a table, and the severity of a rule is the worst severity among the kinds of the rule (values: severity)
- targets: what the rule reads its inputs as. The rule reads an action.yml (an input of action-metadata) by itself, as the steps of a job that calls the action. When the inputs are the whole repository and hold every caller of the action, the rule reads the action on the events of the callers. Otherwise, such as when the inputs are some files of the repository or a caller is in another repository, the rule reads the action on every event that the rule checks for an attacker, the worst case (values: input-kind)
- quality rule: a rule whose finding alone gives no attacker a gain (values: gain): an attack needs another flaw. The flaw that a quality rule finds may still let an attack through another flaw give the attacker more, or keep a vulnerability unfixed for longer. The quality rules check reliability and maintainability. A quality rule has no threat, no CVSS and no severity. The findings of a quality rule set no bit of the exit code; the findings of the other rules, of every certainty, and the inputs set the bits as in a run without the quality rules
- default run: whether the rule runs in a run without --rule (a run that names no rule, or a run of --skip-rule): always, named, facts or given-facts, then what the value means. The default run of a rule holds in a run when the value lets the rule run in that one run: facts and given-facts hold in one run and not in another. sisakulint leaves out of a run without --rule each rule whose default run does not hold in the run, and the report gives the ID of the rule in skipped_rules
- facets: where the rule sorts on each axis, for people to find rules alike; they change nothing the rule reports (values: the heading of each axis in these terms, which is the name of the axis as --explain writes it)
- finding kinds: the kinds of findings the rule reports, each with what it refers to in the rule
- detected: what a finding of the kind says it detects; {name} stands for an argument of the finding
- arguments: under a kind, the arguments of a finding of the kind, each by the {name} that the text of detected writes and what the argument holds; an argument that the text of detected does not name is marked (not in the text of detected), and the JSON output of a finding still has the argument
- consequence: under a kind, why a finding of it is bad
- impact: under CVSS, the highest of the metrics VC, VI, VA, SC, SI and SA (values: CVSS)
- remedy: what a person does about a finding of the kind
- fix kinds: the kinds of fixes the rule may give; under a kind, those a finding of it may give
- fact kinds: kinds of facts about what is outside the inputs, such as a setting of a repository or the commit of a tag: under a kind, those the condition of a finding asks about, which holds only as the facts say; under a fix, those it needs; under a false positive form, those whose answer removes it (values: facts)
- safety: whether a fix may be applied without a person looking (values: safety)
- possible side effects: under a fix, what applying it may change besides the finding, and why a person looks first; a fix given has those of them it makes
- undetected forms: the forms on which the rule reports no finding of the finding kinds under the form, each with the finding kinds and why (disposition). When the finding kinds under a form are every finding kind of the rule, the rule reports nothing on the form, not even an inconclusive finding; when the finding kinds under a form are only some of the finding kinds of the rule, the rule reports a finding of another finding kind of the rule on the form (a finding kind whose conditions the form also meets). The disposition is one of these: no-added-gain, where the flaw that the rule detects adds nothing to what the attacker gets (the disposition no-added-gain does not mean that the workflow is safe); other-rule, where another rule reports a finding on the same form, because the threat of the other rule covers the form; or limitation or todo, where whether the rule should report a finding on the form is not decided, and the consequence of a finding kind of the rule may occur
- inconclusive: the kinds of place that the rule finds and examines, where the rule cannot decide whether the workflow departs from the expected state, or whether the consequence of a finding kind of the rule can occur at the place, because the value or the content that decides the answer is outside what the rule reads, such as a value that an attacker may write, the value of a setting, or the content of a file that the rule does not read (the disposition of an inconclusive kind is limitation or todo: under the disposition limitation, the item with the name decided by gives what decides the answer; under the disposition todo, the item with the name needs gives what the linter would need to decide the answer). On such a place the rule reports a finding whose certainty is inconclusive (an inconclusive finding): the output of a run lists the inconclusive findings among the findings, marked inconclusive, and a count of findings includes the inconclusive findings. The kind of an inconclusive finding is the inconclusive kind, written &lt;rule>.&lt;kind>, in the same form as the ID of a finding kind, and the severity of an inconclusive finding is the severity of the rule (the worst severity of the finding kinds of the rule). An inconclusive finding sets bit 8 of the exit code when the severity of the inconclusive finding is at or above --fail-on, unless an entry of the file of --accept matches the inconclusive finding; an inconclusive finding that an entry matches stays in the output of the run, with the reason of the entry. The disposition of an inconclusive kind is limitation or todo. An inconclusive finding is different from a conditional finding (see confirmed finding, conditional finding): a conditional finding has a condition about facts of a fact kind that the finding kind declares, and the run did not learn the facts; an inconclusive finding has no such condition, and no answer about facts decides an inconclusive finding
- false positive forms: the forms on which the rule reports a finding of a kind though the consequence of the kind does not occur in a workflow that has the form, even when the workflow keeps the expected state, as far as the forms are known: under each form, the kinds of findings of the form, and what the rule would need to stop reporting the form (disposition) or the kinds of facts for which the answer that removes the finding makes the rule report no finding on the workflows that have the form, in the run that has the answer (fact kinds)
- example: an input that shows the declaration, and the kind of input it is (values: input-kind); a test of the rules checks that the rule gives on the example what the declaration says; the name of the file of an example is the ID of the declaration (for an example of several files, the name of its directory is), not a description of what the example has. For a true positive or a true negative, the ID is the ID of the kind without the ID of the rule. A declaration can have more than one example: the main example has the ID alone, and each other example has a label after a dot, as controlled.caller. A true negative of several kinds whose fixed inputs are the same has the IDs of those kinds joined by +, as private+public
- finding on: under an example of several files on which the rule reports a finding, the files where the findings of the declaration are; the first file of the example is the file the declaration is about, and the files of the findings may include the first file, other files of the example, or both
- true positives: under a kind, inputs on which the rule reports a finding of it; the name of the file of an example is the ID of the declaration (for a true positive or a true negative, the ID of the kind without the ID of the rule, and a label after a dot for another example of the kind), not a description of what the file has
- true negatives: under a kind, inputs close to the true positives on which the rule reports nothing and the consequence of the kind does not occur: the input of a true positive, fixed as the remedy says, or an input without a condition that the kind needs. The input of a true negative may also be a form that another rule reports (an undetected form whose disposition is other-rule). An undetected form whose disposition is no-added-gain is a set of inputs on which the rule reports nothing too, declared with the claim why; in the way of no-added-gain where the attacker gets the same without the flaw, unlike on a true negative, the run of such an input can still give the attacker secrets or a token; the name of the file of an example is the ID of the declaration (for a true positive or a true negative, the ID of the kind without the ID of the rule; a label after a dot for another example of the kind, the form or the kind of place, whose main example has no label; for a true negative of several kinds whose fixed inputs are the same, the IDs of those kinds joined by +, as private+public), not a description of what the file has
- provider: under a kind of fact, the value that names where the facts of the kind come from, and what the value means (under each kind of facts in these terms, the line after the provider says how --online answers the facts of the kind)
- answer that removes the finding: under a kind of fact, and under a fact kind of a false positive form, the answer to a fact of the kind that a file of facts or --fact gives so that the rule reports no finding of the false positive forms that name the kind, and when to give the answer; none for a kind that no false positive form names. A run does not answer a fact of the kind with the other answer: when no source answers the fact, a finding whose condition depends on the fact is conditional
- disposition: under an undetected form or an inconclusive kind, why the rule reports no finding on the form or on the kind of place, as the declaration judges now; to decide the disposition is to know whether the rule should report a finding on the form or on the place. Under a false positive form, which the rule does report, the disposition is what the rule would need to stop reporting the form (values: disposition)
- rule: under a disposition, the rule that reports it
- decided by: under a disposition, what decides whether the rule should report a finding on the form or on the place (values: decider)
- needs: under a disposition, what would be added to the linter to decide whether the rule should report a finding on the form or on the place; a user does not add it (values: need)
- added attackers: under an undetected form or a false positive form, the attackers that a run counts only when the user adds the attackers with --add-attacker, such that a run that adds one of the attackers alone reports the findings of the form, and a run that adds none of the attackers does not report the findings. Under an example of a true positive, the attackers such that a run that adds one of the attackers alone reports a finding of the kind on the example, and the run that adds no attacker reports no finding of the rule on the example (values: added-attacker)
- threat: what the kinds refer to: the preconditions, the actors and the incidents
- preconditions: the IDs of the preconditions of the threat of the rule the kind refers to; a finding of the kind does not mean that each of these preconditions holds on the input of the finding (precondition)
- precondition: a statement that the threat rests on, about GitHub, the runner, an action or a program that a job runs, an AI agent, or the repository, by its ID, and the observations or the documents that back the statement. The rule checks some preconditions on the input (such as the events a job runs on) or by a kind of facts (such as repo.wiki-open), and does not check other preconditions; some preconditions are about one form of input only (such as a reusable workflow, which runs on the events of its callers)
- observed: what was seen on GitHub, and the day
- runner: the version of the runner that took part in what was seen
- cites: the documents a statement rests on
- attackers: the attackers of the threat of the rule the kind refers to (values: attacker)
- actor: an attacker (values: attacker), how they go about the attack, the events the attack takes, and what they get
- via: how the attacker goes about it
- events: the events that run a workflow, when the threat depends on them; what each is: GitHub's documentation, https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows
- run starters: who starts the run of each of the events: the attacker by an act of the attacker, or another person or a schedule; in both cases, what the attacker wrote reaches the run (values: run-starter). The value is for an event, not for one run: each event of an actor has one value, by the runs that the attack of the actor takes: attacker when the attack can take a run that the attacker starts by an act of the attacker, even when another person (such as a maintainer who adds a label) starts other runs of the same event; other when the attack takes only runs that another person or a schedule starts (such as the run after a maintainer approves)
- gains: what the attacker gets (values: gain)
- incidents: the IDs of the incidents of the threat of the rule the kind refers to
- incident: a reported attack of what the rule detects, by its ID: the day, and its CVE when it has one
- advisory: the first-hand report of the incident
- compromised: the repositories the attacker changed
- downstream: repositories not changed, but hit through one of those compromised that they use
- CVSS: the CVSS v4.0 Base metrics of each kind and its Exploit Maturity (E), each with why it has its value (values: CVSS)
- vector: the CVSS v4.0 vector of the metrics
- CVSS-B: the score of the kind's CVSS v4.0 Base metrics by the reference calculator of FIRST, and its rating (values: CVSS); for reference, beside the severity, which is found by the table
- CVSS-BT: CVSS-B with the kind's Exploit Maturity (E), the one metric the CVSS specification calls the likelihood of being attacked, and its rating (values: CVSS)
- likelihood: how readily the threat comes about, for the table of severity: the ease of the attack from AV, AT and PR, lowered by AC and UI; not Exploit Maturity (E), which CVSS calls the likelihood of being attacked and only CVSS-BT takes (values: likelihood)
- from: the metrics that give the impact, or that give the likelihood by the row of the table they match
- lowered by: the metrics that lowered the likelihood one step (the rows: values of likelihood)
- reason: why the metric has its value
- citations: the documents the rule rests on: those of the rule as a whole, then those its text cites

## words in the texts

- privileged event: an event that one without write access to the repository triggers, whose payload has what an attacker wrote, and whose run can have the secrets of the repository and a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes: check_run, check_suite, discussion, discussion_comment, fork, issue_comment, issues, pull_request_review, pull_request_review_comment, pull_request_target, status and workflow_run. Among the events that are not privileged events: pull_request, whose author can change the workflow; push and merge_group, which need write access; workflow_dispatch, which one with write access to the permission Actions dispatches; the credential premise keeps such a one in the threat model. The values of the event that the one who dispatches the workflow writes are only the inputs, which the rules report as the inconclusive kind input-dispatch (the decider dispatcher); schedule, which no person triggers; watch, whose payload has no text that an attacker wrote, only the account that starred the repository; gollum, which one without write access triggers only where anyone may edit the wiki (a rule that reads gollum declares gollum: a kind of finding on repo.wiki-open, or an undetected form). The precondition privileged-event is about three of the privileged events: pull_request_target, workflow_run and issue_comment. The Actions policies of a repository can block the runs of any event. GitHub adds to a public repository without an applicable event policy a default policy that blocks pull_request_target. The rules assume that the runs of a privileged event start. For status, check_suite and check_run, the rules assume one more thing: an app outside GitHub Actions, such as an outside CI, makes a commit status or a check run for a commit whose message an attacker writes (a commit of a pull request from a fork, or a commit that merges a pull request), and the commit status or the check run starts a run of status, check_suite or check_run, which runs the workflow of the default branch, whatever branch the commit is on. The payload of a run of any of the three events has the SHA of the commit, and the payload of a run of status or check_suite also has the message, the author name and the committer name of the commit. The rules ask whether an app outside GitHub Actions makes a commit status or a check run for a commit of a pull request from a fork by the fact kind repo.fork-pr-app-checks, and for a commit that the merge of a pull request puts in a branch of the repository or that a merge queue of the repository makes by the fact kind repo.merge-commit-app-checks (a finding whose condition depends on one of the two fact kinds is conditional when no source answers the fact), only for a workflow whose on has only events among status, check_suite and check_run (one, two or all three). For pull_request_review and pull_request_review_comment, the rules assume two more things. First, the repository has an open pull request from a branch of the repository, or a branch from which the attacker can open a pull request: anyone with read access to a repository can open a pull request between two branches that the repository already has, without write access. Second, the run of a review that an outside contributor writes on such a pull request does not wait for an approval, whatever the repository requires of the runs of outside contributors; the runs that the authors of the linter saw were in a repository that requires an approval only for first-time contributors. That a run of a review of a pull request that one without write access opened between two branches that others pushed to the repository has the secrets and the token that the workflow asks for is inferred: the runs that the authors of the linter saw were of reviews of a pull request that the owner of the repository opened. Only for pull_request_target do the rules ask whether the runs start, by the fact kind repo.pull-request-target-allowed (a finding whose condition depends on the fact kind is conditional when no source answers the fact), and only for a workflow whose on has pull_request_target and no other event (no workflow_call event either)
- $/: a uses that starts with \$/, the self repository reference of GitHub: the action at the path after \$/, in the repository of the file that has the uses, at the commit of the running workflow or action; a \$/ uses has no @ and no ref. GitHub documents the reference in https://github.com/github/docs/blob/5815d11586b0796688963a98c889680e60d72dc4/content/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax.md
- tag mode, agent mode: the two modes of claude-code-action. A step with track_progress true, on pull_request, issues, issue_comment, pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment, runs in the tag mode, and a step with track_progress true on another event stops with an error. Otherwise, a step with the input prompt runs in the agent mode, which gives the prompt to the agent; and a step without prompt, on an event of an issue, a comment or a review that has the trigger of the step (@claude, or the label or the assignee that the step names), runs in the tag mode; a step without prompt and without the trigger runs in the agent mode, which starts no agent without a prompt. In the tag mode, the action puts the title, the body and the comments of the issue or of the pull request in the prompt. The tools that the agent has by default differ between the two modes. The code of claude-code-action that decides the mode and writes the prompt: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-action/blob/6fed3ca145920b639991cb756090506e1bcaf515/src/modes/detector.ts and https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-action/blob/6fed3ca145920b639991cb756090506e1bcaf515/src/create-prompt/index.ts
- larger runner: a runner that GitHub manages, with more resources than the standard GitHub-hosted runners; larger runners can be put in runner groups. GitHub documents larger runners in https://github.com/github/docs/blob/5815d11586b0796688963a98c889680e60d72dc4/data/reusables/actions/about-larger-runners.md
- internal repository, enterprise: an enterprise is an account of GitHub whose administrators manage the policies and the billing of several organizations; an internal repository is a repository that every member of the enterprise can read, owned by an organization of the enterprise. GitHub documents them in https://github.com/github/docs/blob/5815d11586b0796688963a98c889680e60d72dc4/content/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/about-repositories.md and https://github.com/github/docs/blob/5815d11586b0796688963a98c889680e60d72dc4/content/get-started/learning-about-github/types-of-github-accounts.md
- input: the word has two meanings. In the definitions of the item names of these terms, and where a text speaks of the inputs, of an input kind or of what is among the inputs, an input is a file given to the linter: a workflow or an action metadata file (values: input-kind). In the other texts of the rules, an input is an input of GitHub: an input of an action (what a step gives the action under with, such as the input prompt of claude-code-action), an input of a reusable workflow, of workflow_dispatch or of workflow_call, or a value of the inputs context (inputs.&lt;name>)
- confirmed finding, conditional finding: two of the three certainties of a finding (the field certainty of a finding in the JSON output); the third certainty is inconclusive (see inconclusive). Some finding kinds have a condition about facts (fact kinds), such as whether anyone may edit the wiki of the repository. A run asks the following sources about a fact in this order, and uses the first answer: --fact, a file under --root, the file of --facts, and the GitHub API (--online). When no source answers a fact, the fact is not known: the run gives a fact no value that no source gave. A confirmed finding is a finding without a condition, or a finding whose condition holds by the answers. A conditional finding is a finding whose condition the run cannot decide, because no source answered a fact of the condition; the output of the run lists a conditional finding among the findings, as a finding that holds if the condition holds. A conditional finding is different from an inconclusive finding (see inconclusive): an inconclusive finding has no condition about facts. When the answers show that the condition does not hold, the rule reports no finding. A confirmed finding sets bit 1 of the exit code, and a conditional finding sets bit 2 of the exit code, when the severity of the finding is at or above --fail-on; a finding of a quality rule has a certainty too, and sets no bit
- credential premise: The threat model assumes the following about the credentials of every attacker. What a credential can change: a credential can change the repository whose files the linter reads only in the ways that the credential allows. For a token (a fine-grained personal access token, an installation access token or a user access token of a GitHub App, or a GITHUB_TOKEN), the permissions of the token decide the changes; a user access token of a GitHub App has only the permissions that both the user and the GitHub App have. For the web interface, for a personal access token (classic) with the scope repo, and for a personal access token (classic) with the scope public_repo in a public repository, the role of the account in the repository decides the changes. The premise: no attacker has, when the attack starts, a credential of either of the following two kinds. The first kind is a credential that can make at least one change in the repository that is allowed neither by the role read nor by write access to the permission Actions. The second kind is a credential with which a required reviewer of an environment of the repository can approve a deployment to the environment. Examples of credentials of the first kind: a token with write access to the permission Contents, Issues, Pull requests, Discussions or Deployments of the repository, or with write access to any other permission of the repository that allows a change and is not Actions; and a credential of an account with the role triage or above. A change of a workflow file needs write access to both the permission Contents and the permission Workflows; write access to the permission Workflows alone allows no change. What the role read can change: the changes that an account with the role read can make depend on the repository and on the settings of the repository, so the boundary of the premise depends on the repository and on the settings of the repository too. For example, an account with the role read can open an issue when the repository has issues enabled, and can open a pull request from a fork when the repository allows forking. In a public repository, any account, also an account without a role in the repository, can fork the repository, and can open an issue, comment on a pull request and open a pull request unless the repository uses the GitHub feature that limits interactions, which can stop opening issues, commenting and creating pull requests. The examples of the role read and of a public repository are not a complete list of changes. Who has the credential: the premise is the same whether the credential is a token that leaked or a credential of a bot, an app or an account of a third party. Attackers that the threat model includes: every attacker whose credentials are of neither kind, for example an attacker whose credentials can make only the changes that an account with the role read can make, and an attacker who also has a credential whose only write access is to the permission Actions. A credential whose only write access is to the permission Actions can dispatch a workflow with inputs of the choice of the attacker, start a re-run (also with debug logging), approve a workflow run that GitHub holds for approval because a pull request from a fork started the run (this approval is not a review of the pull request), change the template of the OIDC subject claim, and delete a workflow run or the logs of a workflow run, among other changes that write access to the permission Actions allows. A credential whose only write access is to the permission Actions cannot push, add a label or approve a deployment with the credential; a workflow that the credential dispatches or re-runs does what the workflow does with the token of the run. What a rule counts: for each attacker, a rule counts what a flaw of the workflow gives the attacker beyond what the credentials of the attacker give the attacker without the flaw. Credentials that a flaw gives: a flaw can give an attacker a credential of the first kind, such as a token that a run leaves in an artifact, or can give the attacker the use of such a credential, such as a workflow that adds a label with a personal access token, or sends a repository_dispatch with a token of the repository, from values that the attacker wrote. With such a use, the attacker does not get the token, but the values of the attacker decide what the workflow does with the token. The premise concerns the credentials that an attacker has when the attack starts, so the premise does not stop a rule from reporting such a flaw; the rule artipacked reports a token left in an artifact. A consequence of the premise: some runs start only after a gate, a label or an approval admits the run. When a person or a program admits the run with a credential that the premise excludes, and no flaw that gives the use of the credential causes the act that admits the run, the rules do not take the person or the program as an attacker, and report no finding whose attack needs the gate, the label or the approval to admit a run that an attacker started. Two cases follow from this consequence and are not further exclusions. In the first case, an attacker took over a bot, an app, an account or a required reviewer whose credential admits the run; the rules report no such finding for the run. In the second case, an attacker has a token of an account with the role write, and the only write access of the token is to the permission Issues. The premise excludes the token, because the token can add a label to an issue, which an account with the role read cannot do. A comment written with the token starts a run whose actor is the account, and a gate that checks the role of the account admits the run; the rules report no such finding for the run. GitHub lists the permissions of tokens in the pages "Permissions required for fine-grained personal access tokens" (data: https://github.com/github/docs/blob/5815d11586b0796688963a98c889680e60d72dc4/src/github-apps/data/fpt-2026-03-10/fine-grained-pat-permissions.json) and "Permissions required for GitHub Apps" (data: https://github.com/github/docs/blob/5815d11586b0796688963a98c889680e60d72dc4/src/github-apps/data/fpt-2026-03-10/server-to-server-permissions.json).
  - R: the repository whose files the linter reads
  - Allow(p): the set of changes that the access p to a permission of R allows
  - RoleOps(R, r): the set of changes that an account with the role r can make in R; the settings of R change the set
  - AnyOps(R): the set of changes that every account can make in R; the set is empty when R is private
  - ReadOps(R) = RoleOps(R, read) ∪ AnyOps(R)
  - ActionsOps = Allow(write access to Actions)
  - Ops(c) for a token c: the union of Allow(p) over the permissions p of c; the permissions of a user access token of a GitHub App are those that both the user and the GitHub App have
  - Ops(c) for the web interface or a personal access token (classic) c: RoleOps(R, the role of the account of c)
  - Reviewer(c): true when a required reviewer of an environment of R can approve a deployment to the environment with c
  - Excluded(c) ⇔ (Ops(c) ∖ (ReadOps(R) ∪ ActionsOps) ≠ ∅) ∨ Reviewer(c)
  - A: the set of the credentials that the attacker has when the attack starts
  - W: the set of the flaws of the workflow
  - Gets(X, F): what an attacker with the set of credentials X gets from a workflow with the set of flaws F
  - the premise: ∀ c ∈ A: ¬Excluded(c)
  - what a rule counts, for each attacker and each flaw f ∈ W: Gets(A, {f}) ∖ Gets(A, ∅)
  - the consequence: when a gate, a label or an approval admits a run by an act with a credential c, Excluded(c), and no flaw of W causes the act, the rules report no finding whose attack needs the gate, the label or the approval to admit a run that an attacker started
- example notes: the comments that the file of an example starts with, each in the form # key: text, which are in the text of the example that --explain writes. The keys: situation: what the workflow of the example does; reason: why the example is what the declaration says: whether harm can occur, why the rule does not detect the example, or why the rule cannot decide; cause: for a false positive form or an undetected form, the part of the rule that reads the example otherwise than GitHub runs the example; attack: what an attacker does, when the attack is not a string that the attacker writes; attack-value: the string that an attacker writes, and the place where the string goes; attack-run-behavior: what the run of the example does when the attack goes in; advisory: the page of an advisory whose workflow the example reproduces steps of: a page of GitHub Security Lab, of the GitHub Advisory Database, or of the security advisories of a repository; one line for each advisory; source: the file of a public repository at a commit whose steps the example reproduces, for a form that no advisory reports: a URL of github.com with blob, the commit and the path of the file, not a branch or a tag; one line for each file; added-attacker: for a true positive, an added attacker (values: added-attacker) such that a run of the linter that adds the added attacker alone reports a finding of the kind on the example, and the run of the linter that adds no attacker reports no finding of the rule on the example; one line for each added attacker. The note reason is not the reason of a CVSS metric (the item name reason)
- fix: a change to a file given to the linter, made of edits of the text of the file, that a rule computes for a finding. For each finding that has a fix, the output of a run shows the fix. --fix writes the safe fixes (see safety) into the files given to the linter, and --fix=review writes every fix, without asking. With --dry-run, no file given to the linter changes. Before the linter writes the fixes, the linter runs the rules again on the fixed text. The linter writes no fix into any file when two fixes overlap, or when the rules on the fixed text still report a finding that a fix was to remove, report a new finding, or change the certainty or the condition of a finding. Without --fix, no file given to the linter changes. A fix is different from the remedy of a finding kind: the remedy is what a person does about a finding

## values

### attacker

- maintainer-of-called: The maintainer of the action or reusable workflow called, or whoever takes over a maintainer's account.
- anyone-who-forks: Anyone who can fork the repository whose files are given to the linter: on a public repository, anyone with a GitHub account; on a private repository where the owner of the repository permits forking, those who have any of the roles read, triage, write, maintain and admin in the repository.
- forker-of-called: Anyone who can fork the repository of an action that a workflow calls; the attacker needs no access to the repository whose files are given to the linter.
- fork-pr-author: The author of a pull request from a fork: they write its title, its body and the name of its branch, and the message, the author name and the committer name of each commit of the pull request.
- issue-author: Anyone who can open an issue or a discussion; on a public repository, anyone.
- commenter: Anyone who can comment on an issue, a pull request or a discussion, or review a pull request; on a public repository, anyone.
- merged-commit-author: The author of a commit merged from a pull request: they write its message and its author's name.
- wiki-editor: Anyone who can edit the wiki: by default those who can write to the repository; anyone with an account on GitHub where the repository allows it (a public repository only).
- artifact-reader: Anyone who can download the artifacts of the repository's runs: signed in to GitHub with read access; on a public repository, anyone with an account.
- image-publisher: Whoever can push to the repository of an image in its registry: its maintainer, or whoever takes over their account or a token that pushes to it.
- repository-reader: Anyone who can read the files of the repository: on a public repository, anyone; on a private one, those with read access, the apps given its contents, whoever has their tokens, and those who kept a clone.
- log-reader: Anyone who can view the logs of the repository's workflow runs: signed in to GitHub with read access; on a public repository, anyone with an account.
- advisory-attacker: Whoever an advisory of the GitHub Advisory Database says can exploit the vulnerability it describes: who that is differs from one advisory to another.
- destination-holder: Whoever runs the server of a destination the workflow names, or takes it over: a breached vendor, or whoever registers a lapsed domain.

### run-starter

- attacker: The attacker starts it by an act of their own: they open, comment, push to their pull request, fork or edit the wiki; or it follows a run of theirs, or a bot they have act starts it.
- other: Someone else's act starts it (a maintainer merges, puts in the merge queue, dispatches or labels) or a schedule does; what the attacker wrote reaches it.

### gain

- run-code: Their code runs in the job.
- read-secrets: They read the job's secrets and its GITHUB_TOKEN.
- write-with-token: They write what the job's GITHUB_TOKEN may write: pushes, releases, packages.
- write-cache: They save entries to the cache of the default branch's scope, which later runs of the repository restore and use.
- set-env: They set environment variables of the steps after this one in the job, and so what those steps run.
- set-outputs: They set outputs of the step, which the steps and the jobs after it take as its own.
- set-path: They choose a directory of the PATH of the steps after this one in the job, and so what those steps run for a command they call by name.
- persist-on-runner: Their code stays on a self-hosted runner and runs beside the jobs that come after it there: it reads their secrets and tokens, changes what they build, and reaches the runner's network.
- use-registry-account: They sign in to a registry as the account whose password is written: they pull its private images and push what it may push.
- reach-runner-network: Requests from the job reach the hosts the runner reaches and the attacker does not: services of a self-hosted runner's network.

### weakness

The kind of flaw of a workflow through which what an attacker does becomes harm.

- script-injection: A string an attacker writes is read as a script, put into it by \${{ }}.
- argument-injection: A string an attacker writes begins a word a command gets, and the command reads the word as an option; the option makes the command run a program or code that is written after the name of the option.
- request-forgery: An attacker's value decides where a request of the job goes.
- environment-file-injection: A string an attacker writes is written to an environment file (\$GITHUB_ENV, \$GITHUB_OUTPUT, \$GITHUB_PATH).
- untrusted-code-execution: A run executes code or a file an attacker made: the tree of a pull request, or an artifact.
- agent-hijack: An AI agent follows what an attacker writes, or holds capabilities wide enough for an attacker to use.
- gate-bypass: An attacker passes a check meant to stop them: an if, or the check of who started the action of an AI agent.
- untrusted-reference: What a workflow refers to (an action, an image) can be replaced by someone else.
- credential-leak: A credential is put where others read it: an artifact, the text of the workflow, the log of a run, or a request to a host the workflow names.
- excessive-privilege: A run holds more permissions or secrets than it needs, or holds them where the event of an attacker reaches; it widens the harm of the other weaknesses.
- workflow-command-injection: A string an attacker writes is printed to the log of a step that allows the set-env and add-path commands, and the runner reads the string as a set-env or add-path command.

### attack-means

What an attacker puts into the run.

- string: A string that reaches \${{ }} or an AI agent.
- code: Code or files: the tree of a pull request, or an artifact.
- operation: An act: moving a tag, pushing after an approval, a commit in a fork, publishing an image, making Dependabot start a run.
- none: Nothing into the form the rule detects: they read what leaked, or use a run they got through another weakness.

### disposition

- no-added-gain: on a form of this value, the flaw that the rule detects (the problem of the rule) adds nothing to what the attacker of the threat of the rule gets from the repository of the input. A form has this value in one of two ways. In the first way, the form does not have the flaw, or the flaw on the form gives the attacker nothing. In the second way, the attacker gets the same without the flaw, such as the author of a pull request, who can change the workflow of a pull_request run when only the pull requests of the repository run the workflow; in the second way, the run can give the attacker secrets or a token that writes, and the workflow can be dangerous while the rule reports nothing. A quality rule has no threat, so no form of a quality rule has this value. The value says nothing of the threats of other rules: another rule may report a form of this value, and the value does not mean that a workflow with the form is safe. The gain that the rule counts is what the attacker gets in the step with the flaw and after that step: in the later steps of the job with the flaw, through the environment files that the step writes, the files that the step leaves on the runner and the processes that the step leaves running; in the other jobs of the run, through the outputs of the job with the flaw and the artifacts that the job with the flaw uploads; and in later runs, through a cache that the run with the flaw saves and a later run restores, and an artifact that the run with the flaw uploads and a later run downloads. What the attacker gets from the repository without the flaw depends on the credentials of the attacker, which the credential premise bounds
- other-rule: another rule reports the same form, as a form of the threat of that rule (rule)
- limitation: nothing that can be added is expected to decide it now; the decider that decided by names decides it
- todo: adding what needs names is expected to decide it for some of its places

### need

- same-file: More analysis of the same file by the linter, not a change that a user makes: reading parts of the file that the rule does not read now (keys, expressions, scripts), such as following an expression, what a script writes to \$GITHUB_OUTPUT or \$GITHUB_ENV, the credentials of the container of a job, or a scope of permissions.
- repo-file: A file of the repository that is not the input: an action.yml, a reusable workflow, a workflow that calls this one, or a file of settings such as .github/dependabot.yml.
- fact: A fact asked of the world outside the input (actions/facts): an action.yml of another repository, a setting of the repository, a registry.
- pin-update: An update of the pinned upstream schemas that the tables of the analysis are made from: the workflow schema and GitHub's webhooks.

### added-attacker

An attacker that the rules do not count in a run of the linter by default, and that a run of the linter counts when the user adds the attacker with --add-attacker. Each value names one credential that the attacker holds, and says which ifs, approvals and checks the attacker gets past, and does not get past, with the credential.

- read-member: The attacker holds an account that is a member of the organization that owns the repository or a collaborator of the repository, and that has the read role in the repository. The account cannot push to the repository. A run of the linter that adds this attacker lets the attacker past an if that compares author_association with MEMBER or COLLABORATOR. The run does not let the attacker past an approval by a label on a pull request, an approval by the required reviewers of an environment, or the check of claude-code-action that the actor can write to the repository. The check of claude-code-action counts the read role as no write access. A finding that appears only because of this attacker has the severity and the texts of its finding kind, written for an attacker outside the repository.
- triage-account: The attacker holds an account that has the triage role in the repository. The account can add a label that the repository has to an issue or a pull request, cannot create a label, and cannot push to the repository. A run of the linter that adds this attacker lets the attacker past an if that compares author_association with MEMBER or COLLABORATOR, and past an approval by a label on a pull request. The run does not let the attacker past an approval by the required reviewers of an environment, or the check of claude-code-action that the actor can write to the repository. The check of claude-code-action counts the triage role as read access. A finding that appears only because of this attacker has the severity and the texts of its finding kind, written for an attacker outside the repository.
- writer-pull-requests-token: The attacker holds a token of an account that has the write role or a higher role in the repository. The token is a fine-grained personal access token or a user access token of a GitHub App, and the only permission of the token with write access is the Pull requests permission (the token may have read access to other permissions). With the token, the attacker can comment on a pull request, review a pull request and add a label to a pull request, and cannot open an issue, comment on an issue or push. In a workflow run that a comment, a review or a label that the token writes starts, a run of the linter that adds this attacker lets the attacker past an if that compares author_association with OWNER, MEMBER or COLLABORATOR, past an if that compares the actor with a name (the linter reads the actor as an account that may have any name that the workflow writes), past an approval by a label on a pull request, and past the check of claude-code-action that the actor can write to the repository. A finding that appears only because of this attacker has the severity and the texts of its finding kind, written for an attacker outside the repository.
- writer-issues-token: The attacker holds a token of an account that has the write role or a higher role in the repository. The token is a fine-grained personal access token or a user access token of a GitHub App, and the only permission of the token with write access is the Issues permission (the token may have read access to other permissions). With the token, the attacker can open an issue and comment on an issue, and cannot comment on a pull request, review a pull request, add a label to a pull request or push. In a workflow run that an issue or a comment that the token writes starts, a run of the linter that adds this attacker lets the attacker past an if that compares author_association with OWNER, MEMBER or COLLABORATOR, past an if that compares the actor with a name (the linter reads the actor as an account that may have any name that the workflow writes), and past the check of claude-code-action that the actor can write to the repository. The run does not let the attacker past an approval by a label on a pull request, because the token cannot add a label to a pull request. A finding that appears only because of this attacker has the severity and the texts of its finding kind, written for an attacker outside the repository.
- required-reviewer: The attacker holds an account that is a required reviewer of an environment of the repository, and that has the read role or the triage role in the repository. The account cannot push to the repository. A run of the linter that adds this attacker lets the attacker past the approval by the required reviewers of every environment that a job of the repository names, because the linter does not know which environments the attacker reviews, and past an if that compares author_association with MEMBER or COLLABORATOR. The run does not let the attacker past an approval by a label on a pull request, or the check of claude-code-action that the actor can write to the repository. For a reviewer with the triage role, add triage-account too, which gets past an approval by a label on a pull request. A finding that appears only because of this attacker has the severity and the texts of its finding kind, written for an attacker outside the repository.
- app-installation-token: The attacker holds an installation access token of a GitHub App that is installed on the repository, with write access to both the Issues permission and the Pull requests permission. The token cannot push to the repository. The actor of a workflow run that the token starts is the name of the App followed by &#91;bot]. A run of the linter that adds this attacker lets the attacker past an approval by a label on a pull request and past an if that compares the actor with a name (the linter reads the actor as an account that may have any name that the workflow writes). The run does not let the attacker past an if that compares author_association with OWNER, MEMBER or COLLABORATOR, because a comment that the token writes has the author_association NONE (seen of comments only), or past the check of claude-code-action that the actor can write to the repository. The check of claude-code-action stops an actor that is not a user unless the input allowed_bots names the actor. A finding that appears only because of this attacker has the severity and the texts of its finding kind, written for an attacker outside the repository.
- variables-writer: The attacker holds a credential that can write the configuration variables that the workflows of the repository read, such as a fine-grained personal access token with write access to the Variables permission. The credential cannot push to the repository. A run of the linter that adds this attacker reads the value of each reference to vars (vars.NAME) as a value that the attacker writes, in any workflow run, whoever starts the workflow run. A finding that appears only because of this attacker has the severity and the texts of its finding kind, written for an attacker outside the repository.
- secrets-writer: The attacker holds a credential that can write the secrets that the workflows of the repository read, such as a fine-grained personal access token with write access to the Secrets permission. The credential cannot push to the repository. A run of the linter that adds this attacker reads the value of each reference to secrets (secrets.NAME) except secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN as a value that the attacker writes, in any workflow run, whoever starts the workflow run. GitHub makes the secret GITHUB_TOKEN for each job. A finding that appears only because of this attacker has the severity and the texts of its finding kind, written for an attacker outside the repository.

### decider

- run-time: What happens when the workflow runs: what a step, an action or an image computes.
- remote-caller: A caller in another repository: a job that calls the workflow (uses: owner/repo/path@ref) and is in a workflow of another repository. The called workflow runs on the event of the run of the calling workflow (github.event_name of the called workflow is the event of the calling workflow), and the calling job chooses the permissions of the GITHUB_TOKEN of the called workflow, the secrets that the calling job passes and the inputs that the calling job gives under the key with. A caller in the repository of the called workflow is not a remote-caller, because the linter can read the files of that repository.
- dispatcher: Whoever dispatches the workflow: the person or the program that creates the workflow_dispatch event, by the Run workflow button, GitHub CLI or the REST API, and chooses the ref and the inputs of the workflow_dispatch event. The value dispatcher is for workflow_dispatch only: no declaration names the sender of a repository_dispatch event as what decides a value. The linter takes the dispatcher as what decides an input of a workflow that has workflow_dispatch, also when the workflow has workflow_call, because a workflow_dispatch run takes any value that the dispatcher chooses. A token that cannot change the files of the repository can dispatch the workflow, such as a fine-grained token that has the permission Actions with write access and no permission Contents (https://github.com/github/docs/blob/5815d11586b0796688963a98c889680e60d72dc4/src/github-apps/data/fpt-2026-03-10/fine-grained-pat-permissions.json, the endpoint create-a-workflow-dispatch-event under actions, with access write).

### safety

- safe: It may be applied without a person looking.
- review: A person looks first.

### severity

How bad a kind's threat is on any repository: the kind's worst case, not the risk to one organization. It is found from cvss by a table, not by CVSS scoring: the impact is the highest of VC, VI, VA, SC, SI and SA; the likelihood is high for AV:N, AT:N and PR:N, medium for AV:N with AT:P and PR:N or with AT:N and PR:L, low otherwise, and AC:H or UI:A lowers it one step (once); impact H is medium, high, critical for low, medium, high likelihood, L is info, low, medium, and N is info.

- info: The impact is N, or L with a low likelihood.
- low: The impact is L with a medium likelihood.
- medium: The impact is H with a low likelihood, or L with a high likelihood.
- high: The impact is H with a medium likelihood.
- critical: The impact is H with a high likelihood.

### likelihood

How readily a finding's threat comes about, for the table of severity: the ease of the attack, from AV, AT and PR, lowered by AC and UI. It is not Exploit Maturity (E), which the CVSS specification calls the likelihood of the vulnerability being attacked: the table leaves E out, and only cvss.bt takes it.

- low: Neither of the rows below; or medium, lowered by AC:H or UI:A.
- medium: AV:N with AT:P and PR:N, or with AT:N and PR:L; or high, lowered by AC:H or UI:A.
- high: AV:N, AT:N and PR:N, and neither AC:H nor UI:A.

### input-kind

- workflow: A workflow: a file GitHub runs from .github/workflows.
- action-metadata: An action.yml or action.yaml: the metadata of an action.
- repo-file: A file of the repository that is not an input: the linter reads the file (such as the configuration of actions/labeler) and does not lint the file.

### facts

- action.definition: The file that defines the action that the runner runs for uses: &lt;repo>/&lt;path>@&lt;ref> (without path, the action at the root of repo), as the archive of the commit that the runner downloads has it. The ref is read as the fact kind git.ref-commit reads it, the tag when a tag and a branch have the same name. In the directory, action.yml when it is a file or a symlink to a file, else action.yaml, else a Dockerfile (or dockerfile). Absent when the archive has none of these there; unknown when the archive cannot be read.
  - provider: github: A GitHub API.
  - --online answers the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- action.runs-using: The runs.using of the action that the runner runs for uses: &lt;repo>/&lt;path>@&lt;ref> (without path, the action at the root of repo). The ref is read as the fact kind git.ref-commit reads it, the tag when a tag and a branch have the same name, and the metadata is read at that commit: action.yml, else action.yaml, at path; with neither, the runs.using of an action with a Dockerfile (or dockerfile) there is docker. Absent when the ref is not there, or none of these files is there.
  - provider: github: A GitHub API.
  - --online answers the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- checkout.executed: Whether a step after the actions/checkout step at step of input_path runs what that checkout brings, reads it as the settings of a tool, or follows a symlink of the tree to a file outside the checkout and puts the content of the file outside the checkout in the log or in an upload that the attacker can read, such as an artifact: a script of the tree, a build or a test that reads its files, an action of it, a file of the tree that a tool reads as settings that decide where a request goes or what command runs (SonarSource's scanner reads sonar.host.url from a project file of the tree and can send a secret to the host that the pull request names), or a symlink of the tree that a tool follows (a parse error of tmatens/compose-lint quotes a line of the file outside the checkout that a symlink of a pull request names). A user answers the fact in a file of facts, with false to say that the tree is read neither as code, nor as the settings of a tool, nor by a tool that follows a symlink of the tree to a file outside the checkout and puts the content of the file outside the checkout in the log or in an upload that the attacker can read; no other source answers the fact. When no one answers the fact, a finding whose condition depends on the fact is conditional.
  - provider: user-supplied: Given by the user.
  - --online does not answer the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: false (write false in a file of facts for a checkout whose tree is read neither as code, nor as the settings of a tool, nor by a tool that follows a symlink of the tree to a file outside the checkout and puts the content of the file outside the checkout in the log or in an upload that the attacker can read)
- dependabot.version-updates: Whether Dependabot version updates read the file input_path for package_ecosystem: whether .github/dependabot.yml (else .github/dependabot.yaml) has an entry of updates whose package-ecosystem is package_ecosystem and whose directory, or one of whose directories, reads input_path. The directory / reads the .yml and .yaml files right under .github/workflows and the action.yml or action.yaml at the root of the repository; another directory reads the .yml and .yaml files right under that directory. An entry with open-pull-requests-limit: 0 does not count. False when neither file is there.
  - provider: repo-file: A file of the repository that is not an input, such as .github/dependabot.yml.
  - --online does not answer the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- download.executed: Whether a step after the download step at step of input_path (actions/download-artifact, dawidd6/action-download-artifact) runs what it puts in the workspace: a script of the artifact, a build or a test that reads its files. A user answers the fact in a file of facts, with false to say that an artifact is only read as data; no other source answers the fact. When no one answers the fact, a finding whose condition depends on the fact is conditional.
  - provider: user-supplied: Given by the user.
  - --online does not answer the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: false (write false in a file of facts for a download whose files are only read as data)
- git.commit-contains: Whether the commit commit is in the history of the commit sha of repo, sha itself included. The API answers it by comparing commit...sha: identical or ahead is true; behind, diverged, or no common ancestor false.
  - provider: github: A GitHub API.
  - --online answers the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- git.commit-ref: A branch or a tag of repo that has the commit sha: its full name. Absent when no branch and no tag of repo has it, as for a commit only in a fork of repo, or a sha that is nowhere. When several have it: the first, in the order of their names, of those that point to sha, else of those whose history has it. A file of facts that has git.ref-commit of repo at sha, found as a branch or a tag, answers it with that ref.
  - provider: github: A GitHub API.
  - --online answers the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- git.commit-tags: The tags of repo that point to the commit sha: their full names, refs/tags/&lt;name>, in the order of their names. An annotated tag is compared by the commit it points to. Empty when no tag points to it.
  - provider: github: A GitHub API.
  - --online answers the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- git.ref-commit: The commit the runner runs for uses: &lt;repo>@&lt;ref>, and the tag or the branch it is found as: the tag named ref if there is one, else the branch, else the commit when ref is its full SHA (with no ref). Absent when none of these is there (a shortened SHA is not resolved: the runner refuses it).
  - provider: github: A GitHub API.
  - --online answers the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- package.advisories: The advisories of the GitHub Advisory Database, of the actions ecosystem, reviewed or malware and not withdrawn, that affect the package package; with version, those GitHub says affect that version (GET /advisories, affects=package@version). One member for each vulnerability of the package: an advisory with several ranges of it has one member for each, not all of whose ranges have the version. Empty when there is none.
  - provider: github: A GitHub API.
  - --online answers the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- renovate.manager-enabled: Whether the configuration of Renovate in the repository enables the manager and has the manager update the file input_path. Renovate reads the first of these files that is there: renovate.json, renovate.jsonc, renovate.json5, the same three under .github/, .renovaterc, .renovaterc.json, .renovaterc.jsonc, .renovaterc.json5, and package.json when package.json has the key renovate. False when none of these files is there. A configuration from outside the repository (a global configuration, an inherited configuration) is not read.
  - provider: repo-file: A file of the repository that is not an input, such as .github/dependabot.yml.
  - --online does not answer the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- repo.action-list: The patterns of the uses that the repository that the linter checks allows its workflows and action metadata files to use: the repository's own policy, which a user writes in a file of facts, in --fact, or in the facts or fact of a configuration file. A uses of another repository or of a Docker image (docker://) that matches no pattern, or matches a pattern that starts with !, is not allowed; a uses of ./ or \$/ is always allowed. The fact is not GitHub's setting of allowed actions, and --online never asks GitHub for the fact. The fact has no argument repo: the fact is always about the repository that the linter checks, so --repo does not change the fact. An empty list allows no uses of another repository and no Docker image. When the repository has no policy, do not answer the fact: leave repo.action-list out of the file of facts and out of --fact.
  - provider: user-supplied: Given by the user.
  - --online does not answer the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- repo.allow-forking: Whether the repository repo (without repo, the repository of the inputs, whose name was not given: no --repo) lets those who may read it fork it. A public repository can always be forked; a private one only when its owner allows it. The REST API gives it of a named repository: GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}, allow_forking. A fact without repo is answered by a file of facts or --fact, and never matches one with repo.
  - provider: repo-setting: A setting of a repository. The API gives some settings and not others (not whether only collaborators may edit the wiki); under each kind of fact, the line after the provider says how --online answers the kind.
  - --online answers a fact of the kind only when the fact names a repository (--repo)
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- repo.allowed-actions: The setting of allowed actions of GitHub that applies to the workflows of a repository: which actions and reusable workflows the workflows may use. The repository is the value of the argument repo; without the argument repo, the repository is that of the files given to the linter, in a run without --repo. The value is the setting that takes effect for the workflows of the repository, with the settings of the organization and of the enterprise that own the repository applied: a repository can only narrow the setting of the organization. GitHub does not start a run of a workflow that uses an action or a reusable workflow that the setting does not allow, and a job fails when a composite action that the job uses has a step whose action the setting does not allow. When a token that can read the Actions settings of the repository (the repository permission Administration, read) is given, --online answers the fact (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/permissions and, when allowed_actions is selected, GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/permissions/selected-actions). GitHub includes the setting of an organization in the answer of the API of the repository: a repository can only narrow the setting of the organization, and the API of the repository then answers the narrowed setting. The authors of the rule did not try whether GitHub includes the setting of an enterprise in the same way. In a run of --online with the GITHUB_TOKEN of a workflow, the token cannot read the setting, and the answer is unknown. For a repository where GitHub Actions is disabled, --online gives the answer absent, and a file of facts or --fact should give the answer absent too. An entry of a file of facts or of --fact without the argument repo answers only a query without the argument repo, and never a query with the argument repo: in a run with --repo, write the argument repo in the entry.
  - provider: repo-setting: A setting of a repository. The API gives some settings and not others (not whether only collaborators may edit the wiki); under each kind of fact, the line after the provider says how --online answers the kind.
  - --online answers a fact of the kind only when the fact names a repository (--repo)
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- repo.archived: Whether the repository repo is archived: read-only, and no longer maintained (all the repositories of an archived organization are archived). The REST API gives it: GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}, archived. Unlike the other kinds of repo., repo is required and is any repository, such as one that a uses names, and the kind comes from the API, not from a setting of the repository of the inputs. The API never answers it absent: GitHub answers 404 both for a repository that is not there and for one the token cannot see, and the answer is then unknown; a file of facts or --fact may answer absent, for a repository known not to be there.
  - provider: github: A GitHub API.
  - --online answers the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- repo.configuration-variables: The names of the configuration variables of the repository level and of the organization level that the workflows of a repository can read in the vars context, without the names of the environment level (repo.environment-configuration-variables). The repository is the value of the argument repo; without the argument repo, the repository is that of the files given to the linter, in a run without --repo. A workflow that reads vars.&lt;name> of a name that no level defines gets the empty string. When a token that can read the Variables of the repository is given, --online answers the fact (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/variables and GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/organization-variables); in a run of --online with the GITHUB_TOKEN of a workflow, the token cannot read the Variables, and the answer is unknown. A repository whose owner is a user, not an organization, has no organization level. The answer holds the names only, not the values. A repository with no configuration variable has the empty list: write the empty list, not absent; for an answer of absent, a rule reports nothing, as for no answer. An entry of a file of facts or of --fact without the argument repo answers only a query without the argument repo, and never a query with the argument repo: in a run with --repo, write the argument repo in the entry.
  - provider: repo-setting: A setting of a repository. The API gives some settings and not others (not whether only collaborators may edit the wiki); under each kind of fact, the line after the provider says how --online answers the kind.
  - --online answers a fact of the kind only when the fact names a repository (--repo)
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- repo.default-token-write: Whether the GITHUB_TOKEN of a job whose workflow and job write no permissions may write, in the repository repo (without repo, the repository of the inputs, whose name was not given: no --repo): the repository's default workflow permissions. The REST API gives it of a named repository to a token that may read its Actions settings (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/permissions/workflow, default_workflow_permissions write); the GITHUB_TOKEN of a run may not. A fact without repo is answered by a file of facts or --fact, and never matches one with repo.
  - provider: repo-setting: A setting of a repository. The API gives some settings and not others (not whether only collaborators may edit the wiki); under each kind of fact, the line after the provider says how --online answers the kind.
  - --online answers a fact of the kind only when the fact names a repository (--repo)
  - answer that removes the finding: false (write false in a file of facts where the default is read)
- repo.environment-configuration-variables: The names of the configuration variables of the environment level of the deployment environment named by the argument environment, of a repository: the value of the argument repo, or without the argument repo, the repository of the files given to the linter, in a run without --repo. A job that names the environment reads them in the vars context in the keys that the runner reads after the job starts (such as env and the keys of the steps), and not in run-name of the workflow or the if and the name of the job. When a token that can read the environments of the repository is given, --online answers the fact (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/environments/{environment_name}/variables); for an environment that does not exist, --online answers the empty list, since GitHub makes the environment with no variables when a job names the environment. The answer holds the names only, not the values. Write the empty list, not absent, for an environment with no configuration variable; for an answer of absent, a rule reports nothing, as for no answer. An entry of a file of facts or of --fact without the argument repo answers only a query without the argument repo, and never a query with the argument repo: in a run with --repo, write the argument repo in the entry.
  - provider: repo-setting: A setting of a repository. The API gives some settings and not others (not whether only collaborators may edit the wiki); under each kind of fact, the line after the provider says how --online answers the kind.
  - --online answers a fact of the kind only when the fact names a repository (--repo)
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- repo.environment-protected: Whether the deployment environment named environment of the repository repo (without repo, the repository of the inputs, whose name was not given: no --repo) has required reviewers, so that a person approves a job that references it before the job runs. A wait timer or a rule of branches is not an approval. Referencing an environment that does not exist makes one with no protection rules. The REST API gives it of a named repository (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/environments/{environment_name}, a protection rule of the type required_reviewers). A fact without repo is answered by a file of facts or --fact, and never matches one with repo.
  - provider: repo-setting: A setting of a repository. The API gives some settings and not others (not whether only collaborators may edit the wiki); under each kind of fact, the line after the provider says how --online answers the kind.
  - --online answers a fact of the kind only when the fact names a repository (--repo)
  - answer that removes the finding: true (an environment is made with no protection rules, so write true in a file of facts for one with required reviewers)
- repo.fork-pr-app-checks: Whether an app outside GitHub Actions, such as an outside CI, makes a commit status or a check run in the repository repo (without repo, the repository of the inputs, whose name was not given: no --repo) for a commit of a pull request from a fork, whose message, author name and committer name the author of the pull request writes. The commit status or the check run starts a run of status, check_suite or check_run, which runs the workflow of the default branch, whatever branch the commit is on. The payload of a run of any of the three events has the SHA of the commit, and the payload of a run of status or check_suite also has the message, the author name and the committer name of the commit. GitHub Actions makes a check run for each job of a workflow run: do not count those check runs, nor a commit status or a check run that a workflow makes with the GITHUB_TOKEN of its run, because GitHub's documents say that events that the GITHUB_TOKEN triggers create no workflow run (the documents name two exceptions, workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch, which are not events of a commit status or a check run). Count a commit status or a check run that a workflow makes with another token, such as a personal access token or the installation access token of a GitHub App, as one that an app outside GitHub Actions makes, because the events of such a commit status or check run start workflow runs. --online never asks GitHub for this fact: the REST API lists the commit statuses and the check runs of one commit, which tells that an app made one for that commit, and does not tell that no app makes one for the commits to come; the REST API lists the installations of GitHub Apps of an organization only to an owner of the organization (GET /orgs/{org}/installations), and gives a GitHub App only the installation of that app (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/installation). A fact without repo is answered by a file of facts or --fact, and never matches one with repo.
  - provider: repo-setting: A setting of a repository. The API gives some settings and not others (not whether only collaborators may edit the wiki); under each kind of fact, the line after the provider says how --online answers the kind.
  - --online does not answer the facts of the kind
  - answer that removes the finding: false (write false in a file of facts when no app outside GitHub Actions makes a commit status or a check run for a commit of a pull request from a fork)
- repo.fork-pr-run-workflows: Whether a private or internal repository repo (without repo, the repository of the inputs, whose name was not given: no --repo) runs the workflows of pull requests from its forks: the setting Run workflows from fork pull requests. A public repository has no such setting, so the fact is absent there. The REST API gives it of a named repository to a token that may read its Actions settings: GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/permissions/fork-pr-workflows-private-repos, run_workflows_from_fork_pull_requests. A fact without repo is answered by a file of facts or --fact, and never matches one with repo.
  - provider: repo-setting: A setting of a repository. The API gives some settings and not others (not whether only collaborators may edit the wiki); under each kind of fact, the line after the provider says how --online answers the kind.
  - --online answers a fact of the kind only when the fact names a repository (--repo)
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- repo.fork-pr-secrets: Whether a private or internal repository repo (without repo, the repository of the inputs, whose name was not given: no --repo) gives the workflows of pull requests from its forks its secrets: the setting Send secrets to workflows from pull requests. A public repository has no such setting, so the fact is absent there. The REST API gives it of a named repository to a token that may read its Actions settings: GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/permissions/fork-pr-workflows-private-repos, send_secrets_and_variables. A fact without repo is answered by a file of facts or --fact, and never matches one with repo.
  - provider: repo-setting: A setting of a repository. The API gives some settings and not others (not whether only collaborators may edit the wiki); under each kind of fact, the line after the provider says how --online answers the kind.
  - --online answers a fact of the kind only when the fact names a repository (--repo)
  - answer that removes the finding: none
- repo.fork-pr-write-tokens: Whether a private or internal repository repo (without repo, the repository of the inputs, whose name was not given: no --repo) gives the workflows of pull requests from its forks a GITHUB_TOKEN that may write: the setting Send write tokens to workflows from pull requests. A public repository has no such setting, so the fact is absent there.
